value.overview: The American Dipper is a stocky, slate-gray songbird specialized for life in fast-flowing streams. It frequently bobs its body while standing on rocks and can walk, swim, and dive underwater to capture prey. It is the only truly aquatic songbird in North America. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly in suitable highland streams, where clear rushing water, rocky channels, and sheltered banks provide feeding and nesting habitat.
value.classification: The American Dipper belongs to the order Passeriformes and the family Cinclidae, the dipper family. Its scientific name is Cinclus mexicanus. The Costa Rican population is generally associated with the southern Central American form often called C. m. ardesiacus.
value.identification: This medium-sized bird is mostly slate gray, with a slightly browner head, dark bill and eyes, pale gray legs, and a short tail that is often cocked upward. Adults of both sexes look alike; juveniles are usually duller and may show pale feather edges. Its constant dipping motion, low flights along streams, and habit of disappearing beneath rushing water are distinctive. A thin white eyelid flash may be visible when it blinks.
value.rangeHabitat: The American Dipper ranges from western North America through Mexico and Central America to Panama. In Costa Rica it is a localized resident of mountainous areas, especially along clear, permanent, fast-flowing streams in the Cordillera de Talamanca and other suitable highland regions. It favors rocky channels with riffles, cascades, waterfalls, boulders, and exposed banks or ledges. Nests may be placed behind waterfalls, on cliff faces, beneath overhanging rocks, or under bridges.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally resident. In Costa Rica, where streams remain open year-round, American Dippers normally stay within or near their breeding territories. Elsewhere, individuals may make short movements downstream, to lower elevations, or between drainages when high-elevation water freezes or food becomes unavailable.
value.breeding: Pairs usually breed beside rushing streams and may defend a linear stretch of water. Both adults help build a domed, moss-covered nest with a side entrance, often on a ledge, boulder, bridge, culvert, or sheltered site behind falling water. The female commonly lays about three to five unmarked white eggs and incubates them for roughly two weeks. Young leave the nest after about three to four weeks and continue receiving parental care afterward.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of aquatic insects and their larvae, including mayflies, stoneflies, and caddisflies. It also takes other small aquatic invertebrates and may eat fish eggs, tiny fish, and occasionally small crustaceans. The bird searches from rocks and stream edges, then plunges into rapids or walks underwater, using its wings for balance and propulsion while probing among stones and submerged vegetation.
value.behavior: American Dippers are strongly tied to flowing water and rarely travel far from a stream. They repeatedly bob or dip their bodies while standing on rocks, sing with a varied, bubbling voice, and fly low along the channel. Their dense, water-resistant plumage and specialized eyes, nostrils, and blood chemistry help them forage in cold, turbulent water. They may roost in sheltered cavities, beneath bridges, or among rocks close to their feeding territory.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered broadly stable, although local populations can be affected by changes in stream quality and water flow.
